title: Count Set Bits
directAnswer: Loop: while n != 0, do `n &= (n-1)` and increment a counter. Runs once per set bit — O(set bits).

remember.takeaway: Each n &= n-1 removes one set bit — count the steps.
remember.formula: count=0; while n: n &= n-1; count++

problemStatement: Given a non-negative integer `n`, count the number of 1-bits in its binary representation (the Hamming weight).
understanding: Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with `n & (n-1)`, counting how many times until n becomes 0.

approaches.name: Brian Kernighan's algorithm
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Count the 1-bits (Hamming weight) with **Brian Kernighan's algorithm**: repeatedly do `n &= (n - 1)`, which clears the lowest set bit, and count how many times until n is 0.

**Why the iteration count equals the bit count.** Each `n &= (n-1)` removes exactly one set bit (the lowest), so the loop runs once per 1-bit. For a sparse number this is far fewer iterations than checking all 32 bits.

**Why it beats the naive 32-iteration scan.** A loop that tests each of the 32 bit positions always does 32 iterations; Kernighan's does only as many as there are set bits — e.g. 1 iteration for a power of two.

**Built-ins exist** (`Integer.bitCount`, `bin(n).count('1')`), but the Kernighan loop is the algorithm interviewers want to see and explains the clear-lowest-bit idiom.
hints: Count how many times you can clear a bit before n is 0.
Why is this better than checking all 32 bit positions?
approaches.insight: Built-ins exist (Integer.bitCount / bin(n).count('1')) but the Kernighan loop is the algorithm interviewers want to see.
approaches.complexityReasoning: one iteration per set bit (≤ 32), each O(1).
